extracted.intended_audience: NIH applicants, peer reviewers, research administrators, and academic scientists interested in NIH peer review integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion of standards, failures, and recommended procedural safeguards for NIH peer review and grant selection, focusing on confidentiality breaches, undisclosed foreign affiliations/other support, collusion, sanctions, and transparency. Aimed at identifying what went wrong and what NIH should do to restore confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidential information handled by peer reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers must not disclose confidential application materials or review information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of prohibited conduct include: disclosing scoring information, sharing study section critiques, forwarding grant application information to third parties, and sharing NIH account passwords. The OIG report highlights cases where reviewers disclosed critiques or scoring and shared passwords. NIH has acted to protect confidential information but the blog argues NIH 'could do more.' Violations have led to termination of review service and other sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure of foreign affiliations and other support
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers and reviewers must accurately disclose foreign affiliations, participation in programs (e.g., China's Thousand Talents), and all Other Support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cites NIH actions against individuals with undisclosed foreign affiliations and notes program staff may detect undisclosed funding through papers that cite undisclosed support. Failure to disclose has resulted in discipline and grants being pulled. Proper Other Support reporting is expected prior to funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue foreign influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent and guard against systematic efforts by foreign entities to influence reviewers and NIH-funded research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH has noted programs by foreign governments (e.g., Thousand Talents) intended to attract scientists and gain access to IP. The OIG report and NIH/FBI referrals were used to identify potential undue influence. The blog emphasizes that foreign-state programs can lead to reviewer misconduct and corruption of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and sanction collusion among reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and address systemic collusion or cartel-like behavior among reviewers that biases scores and funding outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report documented dissolution of two study sections for evidence of systemic collusion among reviewers. Collusion examples include coordinated phone calls to support certain applications and agreement to down-score competitors. NIH dissolved implicated study sections and reassessed affected applications; the blog calls for stronger processes to detect and prevent such behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal sanctions such as 'Do Not Use' flags and terminations
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH should flag and restrict reviewers who breach confidentiality or fail to disclose conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of Nov 2019 NIH flagged 77 peer reviewers as 'Do Not Use' for breaches of confidentiality. Between Feb 2018 and Nov 2019 NIH terminated the service of 10 peer reviewers for undisclosed foreign affiliations plus disclosure of confidential information. 'Do Not Use' prevents participation in future study section meetings until removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassess applications when review integrity is compromised
rubrics_metrics.description: When a study section is dissolved for misconduct, affected applications should be reassessed by different reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH dissolved two study sections (one in 2017 and one in 2018) and reassessed all grant applications that those sections had reviewed. The post questions whether applicants harmed by corrupt review are made whole and calls for transparency about the extent of affected grants and awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage external partners and forensic evidence for detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use national security partners and forensic methods to detect breaches of peer review confidentiality and undisclosed affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH increasingly worked with the FBI; the FBI provided referrals of researchers alleged to have undisclosed foreign affiliations. Forensic evidence (e.g., login records, emails, linked accounts) and monitoring publications for undisclosed support were cited as detection methods in the OIG report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore transparency and institutional accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH must be transparent about investigations and corrective actions to restore confidence in the merit-based review system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post criticizes NIH for soft-pedaling the issue and not fully informing the community (e.g., not responding about 82 peer reviewers). It argues NIH should admit how easily review can be corrupted, explain safeguards, and reassure applicants and reviewers that selection is merit-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent implicit and compensatory bias in reviewer scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not manipulate scores to 'balance the scales' or compensate for perceived systemic bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against reviewers giving favorable scores to their favored approaches or labs to redress perceived institutional or topical biases. This behavior is presented as an anti-pattern that contributes to unfair selection and erosion of trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accountability and follow-through on investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH should provide clear responses and follow-up regarding allegations substantiated by OIG or other partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog questions why NIH did not respond about 82 potentially substantiated reviewers and calls for accountability in reporting outcomes of investigations, including the scope of affected proposals and remediation for harmed applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider procedural reforms to reduce gaming (e.g., lottery safeguards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore structural changes to review/award processes to reduce opportunities for gaming while weighing unintended consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter suggested identifying the top 20% of applications and choosing awardees by lot; the blog replies that a lottery could incentivize large labs to submit many applications. The post argues NIH needs better processes to stop cartel behavior rather than simplistic fixes that may create new gaming incentives.
